statement: A ground loop is formed when two units' signal grounds are tied together in more than one place, for example by the signal cable and by the safety earth; hum occurs when the resulting current flows through a unit's audio signal ground.
AES48 specifies balanced lines with the cable shield tied to the metal chassis at both ends; a balanced line has two signal conductors plus a shield.
locator: RaneNote 110, 'The Absolute Best Right Way To Do It'

statement: XLR pin 1 should be tied to the chassis at the point of entry, not to the audio signal ground.
locator: RaneNote 110, 'The Absolute Best Right Way To Do It'

statement: Transformer isolation is the most reliable way to break a ground loop between balanced and unbalanced equipment.
locator: RaneNote 110, 'The Next Best Right Way To Do It'

statement: If a shield must be lifted, disconnect it at the receiving end and capacitively couple it to the chassis with 0.1 uF or 0.01 uF; this is the hybrid shield termination.
locator: RaneNote 110, 'The Last Best Right Way To Do It'

statement: Any unbalanced cable should be kept under ten feet (three meters); longer cables amplify the side effects of unbalanced ground loops.
Ground-lift switches are band-aids: in most cases they do not improve ground noise and they reduce the unit's ability to be properly grounded.
UL leakage limits are 3.5 mA for 3-prong equipment, 5 mA for 3-prong equipment with a special warning label, and 0.75 mA for 2-prong equipment.
note: Practitioner summary from a presentation, not the standard text. It conflicts with the UL/IAEI summary C187; use the standard for the product class.

statement: Leakage current comes from parasitic capacitances in real equipment, including transformer winding-to-winding capacitance and internal EMI filters, and is a 60 Hz current.
A balanced interface rejects noise through common-mode impedance balance, not through equal-and-opposite signal voltages; this is the definition in IEC 60268-3.

A balanced circuit is a two-conductor circuit in which both conductors and all connected circuits have the same impedance with respect to ground and to other conductors, so noise pickup is common-mode and can cancel in the load.
Common-mode voltage has three main sources: a voltage difference between driver and receiver grounds, magnetic-field induction in the cable, and electric-field induction in the cable.
CMRR is the ratio of differential-mode signal gain to common-mode noise gain, is expressed in dB, and is not a signal level, so it must not be written as dBu, dBV or dBm.
A balanced interface behaves as a Wheatstone bridge; rejecting ground noise requires a precise ratio match of the positive and negative common-mode divider arms.
Real-world common-mode impedances are imbalanced by about +/-10 Ohm at 60 Hz, and the CMRR of the SSM-2141 receiver drops by 25 dB with only 1 Ohm of driver imbalance.
With +4 dBu (1.23 V) reference level, 80 dB of interface CMRR and 15 dB of headroom give 95 dB of total dynamic range, comparable to a CD; 50 dB CMRR is rarely enough for a commercial system.

The pin 1 problem is common-impedance coupling inside equipment that turns the shield connection into a low-impedance signal input, allowing shield current to flow in signal-reference conductors; Neil Muncy named it in 1994.
Good designs give shield current a separate, direct route back to safety ground instead of sharing signal-reference conductors.
Safety grounding must never be defeated to solve a noise problem; doing so is dangerous, illegal in many jurisdictions, and creates liability.
NEC 2008 Articles 250.6(D) and 250.114 prohibit removing safety grounding from plug-and-cord-connected equipment to solve noise issues; signal cables are not safety-ground wiring.
Ground isolators in the signal path are the preferred solution to a ground loop, and their location in the system is critical.

For unbalanced interfaces, keep cables short, use heavy shields, avoid unnecessary grounds, never disconnect safety ground, use isolators at problem interfaces, and separate signal and power bundles by at least 6 inches.
Mesh grounding approximates a ground plane at high frequencies and tolerates loops; star grounding avoids shared conductors and is preferred for audio because 60 Hz is in band.

A ground-lift feature is legally allowed to interrupt safety ground only when the unit provides a GFCI on its output; a premises GFCI outlet must still have its safety ground connected if one is available.
An RCD trips when the active and neutral currents differ by more than a few milliamps; ESP states that most operate at about 20 mA.
note: Practitioner summary for the RCDs ESP describes. Trip thresholds vary by device type and region; see C189 (Class A GFCI, 4-6 mA) and C190 (GFPE, 30 mA or higher).

statement: Disconnecting the safety earth can leave a live chassis if a fault occurs, and may be illegal and expose the installer to liability.
ESP measured about 20 mV of hum induced by transformer stray magnetic field; at 90 dB/W/m and 27 dB amplifier gain this is only 15.7 dB below a 1 W listening level and is very audible.
ESP argues that ground loops are not caused by leakage current because a leakage path from the active line would trip the safety switch instantly.
notes: Contradicts S053 slides 39-40; see references/grounding-shielding.md for the reconciliation using UL leakage limits versus RCD trip threshold.

statement: The correct power-supply earth reference is at the output/regulator end, not at the rectifier; 10 mOhm and 1 uH between two capacitor points produced 42 uV of noise at less than 50 mA.
A 10 Ohm loop breaker reduces a 2 to 5 A shield current, caused by about 1 V RMS between separate earth connections, to less than 200 mA.
An earth wire must not be routed so that it forms a partial or full turn around a transformer; relocate the star point or transformer if necessary.
A transformer core (EI or C-core) and any electrostatic shield must connect directly to chassis and safety earth, not through a loop breaker.

The ground point for a split supply must be taken from the centre tap of the filter capacitors, not from the transformer centre tap, and DC must be taken from the filter capacitors, not from the rectifier.
Capacitance-multiplier wiring should use a star topology, a ground area large enough for all connections but not so large that circulating currents flow, and the shortest possible capacitor leads.
A loop-breaker circuit may not be legal in every jurisdiction; if it is not, balanced interconnects or signal isolation should be used instead.

When a loop breaker is used, all input and output connectors must be insulated from the chassis; otherwise the connector shell provides a direct connection from the zero-volt line to chassis and defeats the loop breaker.
The loop breaker works by adding resistance in the earth return, with a parallel capacitor for radio-frequency continuity and a diode bridge for fault current.

Ground voltage differences between equipment grounds are often caused by magnetic induction in premises AC wiring, not only by voltage drops from leakage currents, and even isolated or technical grounding does not eliminate this mechanism.

In a field case with 30 A rms per phase in untwisted premises wiring, the ground voltage between cable shield pins was about 650 mV rms; twisting the current-carrying conductors reduced it to less than 3 mV rms.
Twisting line and neutral conductors at about five twists per foot gave the lowest induced ground voltage of the tested configurations; the worst case was over 1,000 times worse.
Even in the worst case, leakage currents cannot account for the much higher ground voltage differences observed in the field.

For 50 or 60 Hz sources, UL appliance safety standards limit leakage current to 0.5 mA for portable two-wire and three-wire cord-and-plug appliances and 0.75 mA for three-wire cord-and-plug fixed or stationary appliances; some information-technology equipment with EMI filters may be permitted up to 3.5 mA.
locator: UL Question Corner: Leakage current, paragraph 3
note: UL summary, not the standard text; the limit depends on the product standard and class.

statement: The permitted leakage current on a properly operating UL Certified/Listed cord-and-plug appliance is less than the 4 to 6 mA trip level of a UL Class A GFCI.
locator: UL Question Corner: Leakage current, paragraph 3

statement: A Class A GFCI trips when the ground-fault current is in the range of 4 mA to 6 mA, as specified by UL 943.
A ground-fault protective device for equipment (GFPE) typically trips at 30 mA or higher and is not intended for personnel protection.
